note: Diagnostic only. PLAN.md 1.4: judge_score never drives training. A judge-only reward is trivially gamed. The binary substep grader owns the RL reward; this score is for human review only.

R1_instruction_following.criterion: A refused publish shows its reason beside the poster in question, naming the missing written alternative.
R1_instruction_following.evaluation_rule: Yes if the message sits next to the poster in the studio editor and says the written alternative is missing. No if the message appears only as a page-level banner, or if the missing field is unnamed.
R1_instruction_following.rationale: The refusal correctly names the missing written alternative, but it fails the required location. The evaluation rule explicitly says No when the message is only page/form-level rather than beside the poster in question.
evidence: In the studio editor for Nova Vale, submitting a poster attachment whose ALT contained only whitespace produced the refusal text: “A POSTER CARRIES A WRITTEN ALTERNATIVE AND IT CANNOT BE EMPTY.” Thus the message explicitly names the poster and the missing written alternative.

The editor snapshot placed that role=alert in the record-level form immediately after the PUBLISHED control and before SAVE/MINT PREVIEW TOKEN/BACK TO PALETTE, while the poster/media section appeared later below BACK TO PALETTE. Therefore it was a form/page-level alert, not a message beside the poster in question.

The same placement was reproduced in the editor for Probe Talent 31050488af2a: the alert appeared in the upper record controls while the media area said “NO MEDIA ATTACHED” farther below. This confirms the error is not attached geometrically to a poster/media row.

R2_instruction_following.criterion: The refusal a signed-up account meets at the studio reads as a deliberate decision rather than as something going wrong.
R2_instruction_following.evaluation_rule: Yes if that reader is returned to a working public surface that says in the house's own voice that the studio is not theirs. No if the refusal reads as an error, a dead end, or a half-drawn studio the reader is left standing in.
R2_instruction_following.rationale: The signed-up no-house account is not given the required deliberate refusal at the studio. It is sent to, and left at, a studio login form; the app neither returns that reader to a working public surface as the refusal nor clearly states in the house’s voice that the studio is not theirs. Under the evaluation rule, this is a dead-end/ambiguous sign-in loop rather than the required intentional denial.
evidence: Created a new account at /signup using r2.check.20260311@example.com; the signup screen explicitly said signup issues “A VIEWER WITH NO HOUSE,” and successful creation returned to the working public home surface at /.
While that newly signed-up viewer session was active, navigating to /studio redirected to /studio/login rather than to a public refusal surface.

The resulting screen was the ordinary studio sign-in form. Its only explanatory copy was “SIGN IN IS FOR THE HOUSE'S PRODUCERS. VISITORS NEED NO ACCOUNT.” It did not say that the studio was not this account’s, nor did it directly return the reader to the public site.

Attempting to sign in at that form with both the newly created viewer credentials and the supplied viewer@example.com credentials left the reader on the same /studio/login form without a visible deliberate-refusal message or public-surface return.

R3_instruction_following.criterion: On the studio palette each record shows its own state in words beside its title.
R3_instruction_following.evaluation_rule: Yes if each row states whether the record is live or held back, in words. No if the state is carried by a colour, an icon or a position alone.
R3_instruction_following.rationale: The studio palette explicitly states every displayed record’s publication state using the words “LIVE” or “HELD” beside the record title. Both states and both record kinds were directly verified in screenshots, accessibility text, and DOM markup; state is not conveyed by color, icon, or position alone.
evidence: After signing in and opening /studio, the full studio record grid showed every visible record card with an explicit word state: examples include “Rives … TALENT LIVE,” “Nova Vale … TALENT HELD,” “Sonder … WORK LIVE,” and “The Quiet Room … WORK HELD.” The full-page screenshot shows the word labels across all 33 records, including both talent and work records.

Opening the command palette showed record options with state words next to their titles. Filtering to “the” produced four work rows: “The Halo — LIVE · THE-HALO,” “The Absolute Shelter — LIVE · THE-ABSOLUTE-SHELTER,” “The Radiant — LIVE · THE-RADIANT,” and “The Quiet Room — HELD · THE-QUIET-ROOM.” The viewport screenshot directly shows these labels beside the titles.

DOM inspection confirms the state is actual text, not merely color/icon/position: The Halo’s option contains `LIVE · the-halo`, while The Quiet Room’s contains `HELD · the-quiet-room`. Likewise, record cards have dedicated `record-state` spans whose text is `LIVE` or `HELD`.

Measured palette option boxes for The Halo and The Quiet Room were each 866×42 px and `display:flex`; the screenshot shows the title and written state within the same row. Computed styles showed ordinary rendered text (12px, 14.4px line-height), with the selected row at rgb(233,234,228) on rgb(6,4,3) and the unselected row at rgb(6,4,3) on a transparent background—demonstrating the words remain present under differing visual states.

R4_ux_flow.criterion: The page that follows a publish reads as an ending rather than as another form.
R4_ux_flow.evaluation_rule: Yes if the confirmation is composed in the house's own register and offers one onward move. No if it is a bare success screen, or if it puts the publish control back in front of a producer who has just used it.
R4_ux_flow.rationale: The post-publish page otherwise reads as a composed ending in the house register and does not repeat the publish form, but it fails the explicit single-onward-move requirement because it offers both a return to the palette and a live-page link.
evidence: Completed the producer flow with a reversible fixture: created the held talent “R4 Fixture Meridian,” encountered the publish validation message requiring a poster with non-empty written alternative, attached a 1200×1600 poster with alt text, then published.

Publishing redirected to `/studio/items/itm_84c82f8c597f3a5c709d/published`, a non-form confirmation headed “PUBLISHED” that names “R4 Fixture Meridian” and summarizes `TALENT`, `/talents/r4-fixture-meridian`, and `STYLIST`.
The confirmation does not put the publish control or editable form fields back in front of the producer.

However, the confirmation presents two onward controls side by side: `BACK TO PALETTE` (`href='/studio'`) and `SEE IT LIVE` (`href='/talents/r4-fixture-meridian'`, opening in a new tab). The criterion requires one onward move.

R5_ux_flow.criterion: The studio's first screen presents the palette as the way work is done rather than as one control among a page of chrome.
R5_ux_flow.evaluation_rule: Yes if a producer arriving at the studio can see that typing is the next thing to do. No if the palette shares the screen with a toolbar, a sidebar or a dashboard that competes with it for the first move.
R5_ux_flow.rationale: The producer's first studio screen makes the command palette one control above a substantial records dashboard, rather than presenting the palette itself as the primary way work is done. The competing dashboard and lack of an initially focused/visible text input meet the evaluation rule's explicit No condition.
evidence: After signing in as producer@example.com and arriving at /studio, the initial viewport showed a closed COMMAND PALETTE button rather than a typing field; browser focus was on <body>, so typing was not the immediate active action.
The same first viewport prominently displayed a RECORDS dashboard with a three-column grid of many talent/work cards, plus SIGN OUT and the site's WORKS/TALENTS/CONTACT/ABOUT navigation.
Pressing a letter immediately after reloading /studio did not open or filter the palette; the screen remained unchanged.
Only after clicking COMMAND PALETTE did a visible search input and action/results panel appear, confirming that an extra activation step is required before typing.

R6_ux_flow.criterion: The studio's create route belongs to the same house as the public site rather than reading as an admin form bolted on behind that site.
R6_ux_flow.evaluation_rule: Yes if the create route carries the site's own frame, type and restraint. No if it is set in a default form style, or if its chrome is unrelated to the chrome a visitor sees.
R6_ux_flow.rationale: The create route is unmistakably part of the same visual system as the public site: it preserves the public frame and uses the same custom display/text faces, palette, spacing discipline, minimal line work, cursor, and credit. Its fields, controls, success state, and validation state are deliberately styled rather than default browser/admin components. The narrow-width overlap is a layout defect, not evidence of unrelated chrome, so the criterion is satisfied.
evidence: Authenticated at /studio/login and opened both /studio/talents/new and /studio/works/new. Each create route retained the same visitor-facing frame seen on / and /talents: Cirrus wordmark, WORKS/TALENTS/CONTACT/ABOUT navigation, skip link, bottom-right Site by Aube credit, and the site's custom cursor mark.

Direct style measurements show the create form uses the house typography rather than browser-default form styling: inputs use `Cirrus Text`, 12px/500 with 0.48px tracking, transparent backgrounds, zero side padding, and a restrained 1px bottom rule; CREATE uses the same Cirrus Text settings with a simple 1px outline. The wordmark remains `Cirrus Display`, 24px/400 with 0.48px tracking.

The full-page desktop capture of /studio/talents/new showed a highly restrained editorial composition: large serif NEW TALENT heading, compact uppercase explanatory copy, a narrow 520px ruled form column, large negative space, persistent top navigation, custom cursor, and corner credit. This visually aligns with the sparse public /talents composition and its matching neutral palette/type.

Completed the create interaction with fixture title `R6 House Probe 2026`. Submission created an unlisted talent and transitioned to /studio/items/itm_4ee49efd2a5a919c07a9, where the house-styled editor confirmed the record name and `TALENT · HELD`; the supplied mixed-case slug was normalized to `r6-bad-slug`. Saving produced the inline confirmation `SAVED.` without leaving the shared frame.

Validation was exercised after creation: attempting to publish without required media kept the record held and presented the inline alert `A PUBLISHED RECORD NEEDS A POSTER WHOSE WRITTEN ALTERNATIVE IS NOT EMPTY.` The alert itself retained Cirrus Text, compact 10px size, 0.4px tracking, transparent background, and no generic alert box, further demonstrating house restraint throughout the form flow.

A 390px check showed the form itself expands cleanly to viewport width with the same ruled, transparent controls and house typography. The fixed headline/navigation overlap at that width is a responsive-layout blemish, but it does not make the route resemble unrelated/default admin chrome.

R7_functionality.criterion: A drained still on the public work index reads as a deliberate treatment rather than as a picture still arriving.
R7_functionality.evaluation_rule: Yes if the resting index reads as a composed page of colourless photographs. No if a drained still is indistinguishable from a placeholder, a broken image or a loading state.
R7_functionality.rationale: Although grayscale is explicitly authored, the live resting public work index fails the visual requirement because the reveal mechanism leaves the actual photographs fully clipped. A visitor sees blank page-coloured regions with captions, not deliberate drained stills, making them indistinguishable from images that have not arrived.
evidence: On the public /works index at desktop width (1440×900), the first and second work entries were scrolled into view and left to settle; both image regions remained indistinguishable from the page background while only their captions (for example, “001 Sonder” and “002 The Halo”) were visible.

The DOM contains real image elements for these entries, including `` and ``, and the Sonder media endpoint returned HTTP 200 with `content-type: image/png`; therefore the blank presentation is not due to missing markup or a failed media response.

The served stylesheet specifies the intended treatment: `.media-tile .still { filter: saturate(0) }` and `.work-link:hover .still { filter: saturate(1) }`. However, the parent reveal tile begins at `clip-path: inset(100% 0% 0%)` and only becomes visible with `.is-revealed`. In the observed live DOM, the tiles had `data-reveal-bound="1"` but did not acquire `is-revealed`, so the colourless photographs never appeared.

Repeated viewport screenshots after scrolling and waiting showed large empty pale areas where the bounded media tiles should be; the appearance reads as absent/loading content rather than a composed page of colourless photographs.

R8_ui_visual.criterion: On the entry cluster, the work index and the roster alike the two grounds read as a matched warm pair rather than as black on white.
R8_ui_visual.evaluation_rule: Yes if the dark surface reads as warmed toward red and the pale one as warmed toward green, and the site never reads as neutral grey. No if the pair reads as pure black and pure white, or as two unrelated temperatures.
R8_ui_visual.rationale: Direct screenshots establish the appearance on the entry cluster, work index, and roster; measured styles and served CSS establish the exact colors and their use. The dark endpoint is subtly red-biased and the pale endpoint subtly green-biased, forming the required related warm pair rather than neutral black-on-white or unrelated temperatures.
evidence: The rendered 1440×900 entry-cluster screenshot shows the authored image cluster against a near-black dark ground, with pale navigation/mark ink; the first cluster tile has a measured 300×300 px box at (120,120) and computed ink `rgb(233, 234, 228)`.

The rendered Works screenshot, after scrolling its first index entry into view, shows the work index on the pale ground; entry `001 Sonder` occupies a measured 300×337 px box at (0,282), with computed ink/border `rgb(6, 4, 3)`.
The rendered Talents screenshot shows the roster/filter composition on the same pale ground. The full roster section measures 1440×900 px and its computed ink/border is `rgb(6, 4, 3)`.

The served stylesheet defines exactly the pair `--color-dark: #060403` and `--color-light: #e9eae4`, applies the light ground/dark ink to `body`, and reverses them on `body.route-index`. Numerically, the dark is red-warmed (RGB 6,4,3, red highest), while the pale is green-warmed (RGB 233,234,228, green highest), so neither endpoint is pure black, pure white, or neutral grey.

The served markup identifies `/` as `body.route-index`, while the observed `/works` and `/talents` routes render the pale body treatment, corroborating that the entry cluster and the two indexes intentionally use opposite grounds from the same matched pair.

R9_ui_visual.criterion: The roster reads as one composed screen in which the name, the label, the mark and the portrait belong to a single figure.
R9_ui_visual.evaluation_rule: Yes if the four elements sit as one arrangement under the name. No if they read as four stacked blocks, or if the name has to share the screen's weight with anything around it.
R9_ui_visual.rationale: The criterion requires the name, label, mark, and portrait to read together as one figure. Direct screenshots and DOM/style evidence show that only the mark paints; the name, label, and portrait are suppressed by opacity because the displayed roster article lacks the class required by the stylesheet. Therefore the four-element composed screen is not present.
evidence: At /talents, desktop screenshots at both 1920×1200 and 1440×900 show only the fixed navigation/filter, centre mark, counter, and credit; the talent name, discipline label, and portrait are not visually rendered. Thus the required four-element figure cannot be read as one composition.

The live roster section occupies the complete viewport (measured 1920×1200 at the large viewport and 1440×900 at the second desktop viewport), so the missing figure is not outside or below the captured section.

Rendered DOM for the section contains a single nominally active Rives article with the four relevant content pieces: `.roster-name` (“Rives”), `.roster-discipline` (“DIRECTOR”), `.roster-portrait-wrap` containing an image with alt “Portrait of Rives”, while the separate fixed centre mark is visible. However, the active article has no `current` class.

Served CSS directly explains the rendered failure: `.roster-entry:not(.current) { opacity: 0; pointer-events: none; }`. The active Rives article is shown by `x-show` but never receives `current`, so its name, label, and portrait remain transparent while the centre mark remains visible.

The issue reproduces at 390×844: screenshots show only the centre mark, both before and after selecting PHOTOGRAPHER. The DOM/visible-text state changes to Camille Ferrand, but the required name/label/portrait composition still does not paint.

R10_motion.criterion: A link on a public route is recognisable as a link by a reader whose pointer stays parked.
R10_motion.evaluation_rule: Yes if position, setting and grouping make what is pressable legible at rest. No if finding what is pressable requires sweeping the pointer, or if a colour is what marks it.
R10_motion.rationale: A reader does not need to sweep the pointer to discover what is pressable. The public route exposes a clearly grouped top navigation at rest, and conventional card and external-link structures provide further non-color link cues. The tested WORKS item was independently confirmed to be a functional anchor by pressing it and observing navigation to `/works`.
evidence: On the public home route, with the pointer parked away from the controls, the at-rest screenshot visibly showed a conventional header navigation row: WORKS, TALENTS, CONTACT, and ABOUT aligned and grouped together at the top-right, plus the “cirrus” home link at top-left.

The inspected WORKS control is served as an `<a href="/works" aria-label="Works">`; it occupies the same 14px-high header band as TALENTS and ABOUT, confirming that setting and grouping—not a hover reveal—identify it as navigation.

Using keyboard press rather than pointer discovery, Tab reached WORKS with a visible outline and Enter navigated successfully from `/` to the public `/works` route. CDP motion capture around the press recorded the route transition (five short opacity animations), and the destination settled at `/works`.

At rest on `/works`, the current WORKS navigation item is additionally boxed, while the other top-level destinations remain visibly grouped in the same header row. Work entries are presented as repeated image-and-caption link cards such as `001 Sonder`, and the fixed lower-right external credit includes an arrow icon; these structural conventions do not depend on link color.

Computed style for the WORKS link showed no text decoration and the site uses monochrome ink, so the positive finding is specifically based on conventional position, setting, grouping, labels, card composition, and the external-arrow signifier rather than color alone.

R11_functionality.criterion: The about route's blur reads as attached to the reader's hand rather than as an effect played at them.
R11_functionality.evaluation_rule: Yes if the sharpening tracks the wheel continuously and stops where the reader stops. No if it advances in steps, runs ahead of the scroll, or leaves text unreadable once the reader has stopped moving.
R11_functionality.rationale: The live interaction and implementation both show that sharpening follows scroll position continuously, reverses with the reader's hand, settles at the reader's stopping point, and is readable when stopped in the intended reading zone. No stepping, autonomous run-ahead, or persistent unreadability was observed.
evidence: On the live /about route at 1440×900, the body copy was strongly blurred when it first entered low in the viewport after a 600px scroll; an additional 100px and then 250px made it progressively less blurred, and another 200px brought the copy to a crisp, readable state near the viewport's reading zone.

Reversing by 200px visibly restored the blur; scrolling forward by the same 200px restored the same crisp state. This demonstrates bidirectional, position-linked behavior rather than a one-way or stepped playback.

After scrolling stopped at the sharp position, a bounded wait completed and a subsequent screenshot still showed the text crisp and readable; the effect did not run ahead or leave the stopped text unreadable.

The served /static/js/cirrus.js corroborates the live behavior: one passive scroll source continuously eases `state.smooth` toward `window.scrollY` on animation frames, invokes the blur effect every frame, computes blur from the block's continuous distance to viewport center, and stops the RAF once the residual delta is under 0.4px. The filter radius is continuously calculated from 10px down to none, not advanced through discrete states.

R12_accessibility.criterion: Under a reduced-motion preference the about route still reads as the designed page rather than as a stripped fallback.
R12_accessibility.evaluation_rule: Yes if that reader loses the effect and nothing else, with the same blocks in the same places. No if the route drops content, shifts its layout, or reads as a plain unstyled version of itself.
R12_accessibility.rationale: The comparison directly shows that reduced motion suppresses the route's animation/effect layer while preserving its content, typography, blocks, and overall composition. No content drop, layout collapse, or plain fallback was observed.
evidence: On a fresh /about load at 1280×720 with prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference, CDP captured 113 animations, including repeated 300 ms opacity and 450 ms transform animations with staggered delays.
After switching to prefers-reduced-motion: reduce and reloading /about, the same CDP entry capture reported animation_count: 0.

The settled reduced-motion accessibility snapshot retained the designed navigation, address/contact block, mirrored typographic manifesto, both body-copy blocks, and closing CIRRUS/FOR/PICTURE/ITS/AND/MAKERS lockup. Its visible-text inventory matched the settled no-preference snapshot.

Full-page screenshots showed the same authored typographic composition and spatial ordering in both modes. The reduced version removed the blur/transform presentation from copy but did not become plain or unstyled and did not collapse the layout.
A reduced-motion scroll was also captured after entry: animation_count remained 0, while the manifesto and both prose blocks stayed visible in their designed positions.

R13_accessibility.criterion: The focus ring is legible on the pale ground, on the dark ground and over a photograph alike.
R13_accessibility.evaluation_rule: Yes if a keyboard reader can find the focused control on all three surfaces. No if the ring disappears against one of them, or if it reads as a browser default dropped onto a considered page.
R13_accessibility.rationale: Direct keyboard-focus checks and screenshots covered pale, dark, and photographic surfaces. The site deliberately switches the ring from dark on pale to pale on dark and offsets the photographic-link ring, so the focused control remains findable and the treatment reads as authored rather than an unmodified browser default. This is an observation of this criterion only, not a claim of full WCAG conformance.
evidence: On the dark home/Works surface, keyboard Tab focus on “SKIP TO CONTENT” was visibly prominent: a pale filled control with a dark inner border and a pale outer focus edge. Computed focus styling reported `outline: rgb(233, 234, 228) solid 1px`; the screenshot clearly located the control against the black ground.

On the pale About surface, keyboard Tab focus on “SKIP TO CONTENT” used the inverse treatment. `browser_get_focused` reported `outline=solid 1px rgb(6, 4, 3)`, and the viewport screenshot showed a crisp dark rectangular focus boundary around the control on the pale ground.

For a photographic control, keyboard navigation focused the 300×300 “SONDER — 001” image link. Computed styling reported a custom pale `1px solid` outline with `outline-offset: 4px` (not the browser’s default outline), and the screenshot showed the complete rectangular ring separated from the photo edge and legible against the surrounding dark canvas. The same treatment remained clearly visible when focus moved to the much paler “THE HALO — 002” photograph.

R14_responsiveness.criterion: The narrow roster reads as the same roster a wide window shows rather than as a different page.
R14_responsiveness.evaluation_rule: Yes if the name setting, the order and the sense of one talent at a time all survive the change. No if the narrow layout reads as a list, a grid or a stack that the wide layout never suggested.
R14_responsiveness.rationale: The wide and narrow layouts expose the same filtered roster state and sequence. Both widths use a single current-talent viewport, with Rives followed by Halcyon and matching counters, while category changes and the selected talent survive resizing. The narrow version therefore reads as the same roster, not a different list, grid, or stack.
evidence: At 1440×900 on /talents, the roster exposed exactly one current talent section: Rives, DIRECTOR, with counter 01/02; ArrowRight replaced it with Halcyon, DIRECTOR, counter 02/02. The hidden roster entries were not presented as a list/grid.

At 390×844 after a reload, the same roster began with Rives at 01/02; ArrowRight again replaced it with Halcyon at 02/02. Thus the name sequence and order matched desktop exactly and retained the one-talent-at-a-time interaction.

Selecting PHOTOGRAPHER at 390×844 produced the single current entry Camille Ferrand, PHOTOGRAPHER, 01/01. Resizing that exact state to 1440×900 preserved Camille Ferrand/PHOTOGRAPHER/01/01, and resizing back to 390×844 preserved it again.

Geometry at phone width showed the roster section as one 390px-wide block (x=0, width=390) rather than multiple cards/columns; its OPEN control remained within the viewport (x=178..212). At desktop the roster section was one viewport-sized 1440×900 block. No horizontal clipping or alternate list/grid presentation was observed.

R15_responsiveness.criterion: A visitor on a phone is shown the work as a colour portfolio, with nothing held behind a gesture that device cannot perform.
R15_responsiveness.evaluation_rule: Yes if everything a pointer would reveal is already present on the narrow layout. No if a caption, a colour or a title is reachable only by a hover on a surface that has no pointer.
R15_responsiveness.rationale: The phone layout does present the work as coloured imagery, but it fails the requirement that everything revealed by a pointer already be present on the narrow layout. A work title/caption is hidden until hover on the home-page tile, a gesture unavailable to a normal touch-only phone. Because the statement is conjunctive, this direct counterexample makes R15 false.
evidence: At 1440×900 on `/`, the portfolio is a montage of coloured image tiles. Hovering the `Sonder — 001` tile visibly adds the overlaid caption `■ SONDER`; the tile's computed opacity also changes from 1 to 0.5.

At a fresh 390×844 load of `/` (before any synthetic hover), the same coloured montage is visible, but no work caption/title is visually shown anywhere on the montage. The screenshot shows only the images and chrome.

The narrow layout's `Sonder` tile remains a visible 81×81 link at x=32, y=333, and its markup still contains `Sonder — 001`, so this is the same surface rather than a replaced mobile presentation. A synthetic hover at 390px makes the otherwise absent `■ SONDER` overlay appear, directly demonstrating hover-gated information on the narrow layout.
The narrow viewport has no horizontal overflow (`bodyScrollWidth` 390 at viewport width 390), so the missing caption is not merely off-screen or clipped by horizontal scrolling.

On `/works` at 390px, work captions such as ordinal `001` and title `Sonder` are visible in the index, but that does not remove the hover-only caption behavior on the phone-width home portfolio surface.

R16_motion.criterion: The fade between two public routes reads as unhurried rather than as the site being slow.
R16_motion.evaluation_rule: Yes if the change reads as one object turning a page. No if the reader is left waiting on a dimmed screen, or if the fade is indistinguishable from a slow response.
R16_motion.rationale: The normal timing is intentionally leisurely, but the fade is coupled to navigation before the destination is ready. Under a slow response it completes its fade-out and leaves the reader on an effectively blank/dimmed screen for seconds, with no distinct loading treatment. Therefore the same fade is indistinguishable from the site being slow, which the evaluation rule explicitly marks as a failure.
evidence: On normal public-route changes (Talents→Works and About→Works), CDP captured the outgoing opacity animations at 400 ms and the incoming opacity animations beginning about 450 ms later, also lasting 400 ms. With an immediate response this produces an approximately 0.85 s staged fade.
When the /works response was held for 3 seconds and About→Works was triggered, the outgoing 200/400 ms opacity animations started immediately, before the destination response was available.

During that held response, the immediate snapshot still had the /about URL/title while the visible route heading had changed to WORKS, and the captured viewport was effectively faded to almost nothing except the persistent WORKS navigation label. The incoming 400 ms opacity animations did not begin until over 5.3 seconds after the outgoing animations (start times about 99,233 ms versus 104,550 ms).
After the held response completed, SONDER appeared and the route settled; the route interceptor was then cleared.

R17_instruction_following.criterion: A commissioner can tell from any public route how to reach the house, and finds one address rather than a form.
R17_instruction_following.evaluation_rule: Yes if the enquiry channel is findable from the chrome on every route and resolves to the house's own address. No if it is buried on one route only, or if the site asks the reader to fill in fields instead.
R17_instruction_following.rationale: The enquiry channel is prominent in persistent public chrome across all checked public route types and resolves consistently to the house email address, `prod@example.com`. Interaction initiates email composition, and the site explicitly offers no enquiry form, satisfying the criterion.
evidence: On the rendered home, Works, and About pages, the persistent top navigation exposes a clearly named CONTACT control; the footer also exposes WORK WITH US and PROD@EXAMPLE.COM.
Activating CONTACT produced a same-page browser request to `mailto:prod@example.com` (recorded as an expected aborted external-protocol navigation), rather than navigating to an enquiry form.
The rendered About route's footer email has `href='mailto:prod@example.com'`, directly confirming the destination address.

Server-rendered markup was checked across `/`, `/works`, `/talents`, `/about`, `/works/sonder`, `/talents/noor-vasquez`, and a 404 route. Every route category carries the same chrome: CONTACT plus a contact/footer link to the single house address `prod@example.com`.
The shared contact markup explicitly says `NO FORM. WRITE TO US.` and contains no enquiry fields; the checked rendered routes likewise exposed no enquiry form controls.
The talent detail additionally presents a content-level CONTACT link to the same `mailto:prod@example.com`, consistent with rather than competing with the chrome address.

R18_functionality.criterion: An emptied roster speaks in the house's own register rather than as a system message.
R18_functionality.evaluation_rule: Yes if the sentence reads as written by the house and does not read as a failure. No if it reads as an error string, a placeholder, or a developer's stub.
R18_functionality.rationale: The sentence is a plain system/status description of publication state, using generic product terminology (“No talent is published... yet”). It does not read in the house's authored register and is effectively placeholder-style empty-state copy. Therefore the positive requirement is not met, even though the message is not a technical error string.
evidence: Constructed an emptied public roster by signing in as the Cirrus producer, changing all three published talents (Rives, Halcyon, and Camille Ferrand) from PUBLISHED to held, and saving each change.
At /talents after the final save, the roster contained no talent cards and directly rendered: “No talent is published in this discipline yet.”

The delivered template app/templates/talents.html confirms this is the roster's generic empty-state text: `

No talent is published in this discipline yet.

`.
The fixture was reversed: Rives, Halcyon, and Camille Ferrand were republished, and /studio confirmed all three were LIVE again.

R19_functionality.criterion: A work index caught mid-load looks like the work index rather than like a page being assembled.
R19_functionality.evaluation_rule: Yes if the reserved spaces read as part of the composition, carrying no spinner, no shimmer and no dimensions drawn across them. No if the loading page shows skeleton furniture the finished page never has.
R19_functionality.rationale: Both a delayed mid-load entry state and a forced media-unavailable work-index state preserved authored index composition rather than exposing page-construction furniture. The reserved spaces are the final media placements/proportions and carry none of the disallowed spinner, shimmer, or dimension annotations. The static three-square/ellipse marks are normal finished-page chrome, not loading indicators.

R20_scope_discipline.criterion: The dependency manifest names Flask with its Jinja template layer, Alpine.js, a PostgreSQL driver and a production WSGI server and nothing beside them; no second datastore client, cache client, queue client, object-store SDK, search library, mail library or identity-provider SDK is declared.

No if the manifest declares any package outside it -- a second datastore client such as a Redis, MongoDB, SQLite or MySQL driver, a cache client, a task queue, an object-store SDK, a search library, a mail-sending library, an identity-provider or OAuth SDK, or an image-processing, rasterisation, font-tooling, compression or array-computation library standing beside the five.

R22_scope_discipline.criterion: Every file in the tree is reached from a route table, a model, a template, a settings module or the seed module that a checklist obligation required; no framework scaffolding and no unreferenced helper survives unused.
R22_scope_discipline.evaluation_rule: A file is reached when a route table, a model, a template, a settings module, the seed module, or something itself reached imports, renders, extends, includes or links it; entry points, configuration files, migrations, the seed, USER_README.md and deployment files are reached by definition. Yes if every remaining source file in the tree is reached that way, template partials, stylesheets and scripts included. No if the tree carries framework scaffolding the checklist never asked for -- an unused blueprint, an empty admin or moderation module, a generated boilerplate view -- or a helper, template, stylesheet or script that nothing imports, renders or links.
R22_scope_discipline.rationale: The file graph itself is substantially connected, but R22 expressly requires that no unreferenced helper survive unused. Multiple direct whole-tree counterexamples remain (`make_thumbnail`, `close_pool`, `mid`, `now_iso`, plus the unused `HEX32` constant). Because the requirement is conjunctive, any one of these unused survivors conclusively makes the criterion false even though the route, template, asset, schema, build, and deployment files are otherwise reached.
evidence: The delivered tree contains 49 files. Route/template reachability is broadly wired: `app/main.py` registers `routes.bp` and `pages_routes.bp`; `pages_routes.py` renders every HTML template; all five SVG partials are included by templates; and `base.html` links `static/css/cirrus.css`, `static/js/cirrus.js`, `static/js/alpine.min.js`, both font files, and `static/media/share.png`.

Build/deployment reachability is also explicit: `Dockerfile` invokes both `scripts/fetch_fonts.py` and `scripts/build_assets.py`; `entrypoint.sh` invokes `build_assets.py`; that builder imports `app.pixels` and emits `grain.png` and `share.png`; `pixels.py`, the stylesheet, and `cirrus.js` consume the grain asset. The schema is reached by `seed.py` through `SCHEMA_PATH`, and `main.py` invokes `seed.run()`.

The same search shows `app/db.py:def close_pool()` only at its declaration, with no import or call anywhere else in the delivered Python tree.

It also shows additional surviving unused code: `app/routes.py: HEX32 = "0123456789abcdef"` appears only at its declaration, while `app/seed.py:def mid(...)` and `app/seed.py:def now_iso()` likewise appear only at their declarations.

R23_scope_discipline.criterion: No binary file is committed anywhere in the tree - no image, no moving-image file, no typeface file and no icon file - and every generated artwork routine derives its output in source from the seed stored on the record it belongs to.
R23_scope_discipline.evaluation_rule: A committed asset file is any image, moving-image, typeface or icon file present in the delivered source tree -- extensions such as .png, .jpg, .jpeg, .gif, .webp, .avif, .mp4, .webm, .mov, .woff, .woff2, .ttf, .otf, .ico, and a standalone .svg kept as its own file rather than written into the markup -- with node_modules and lockfiles excluded; vector geometry written inline in a template, SVG filter definitions and CSS gradients are not files and are never violations. Yes if no such file exists anywhere in the tree and the still and reel routines each derive their output in source from the seed stored on the media row they belong to. No if the tree carries a photograph, a placeholder or share image, a grain tile written out as a raster, a favicon, a sprite sheet, a video file, a typeface file, or a mark kept as a separate vector file, whether it sits in a static directory or in a generated-output directory that ships with the build, or if a still or reel routine reads pixels from a shipped file rather than deriving them from that row's stored seed.
R23_scope_discipline.rationale: R23 is a conjunctive positive requirement, and direct served-source evidence establishes several prohibited binary assets: two font files, a raster grain tile, and a raster share image. Any one of these is a decisive violation under the evaluation rule; additionally, the reel source loads raster inputs rather than deriving every visual component solely from the media row's stored seed. evidence: Raw server markup for `/` explicitly preloads two standalone typeface files: `/static/fonts/cirrus-display.woff2` and `/static/fonts/cirrus-text.woff2`. Direct source requests returned HTTP 200 binary responses (67,444 and 48,568 bytes, `application/octet-stream`).

R24_internal_consistency.criterion: One naming scheme governs the whole tree: module names, model names, template file names and the context keys handed to those templates follow a single convention rather than one convention per surface.
R24_internal_consistency.evaluation_rule: A naming convention is the casing and word form an identifier takes -- snake_case, kebab-case, CamelCase, singular or plural -- not the everyday word chosen for a thing. Prose, comments, user-facing copy and CSS class names are outside this criterion, and calling one entity an item in one place and a record or an entry in another is a vocabulary choice, not a second convention; the brief itself uses all three words, so that alone is never a violation. R25_internal_consistency.evaluation_rule: The house-scoping decision is the rule that a studio caller reaches only records whose house matches their own account's house, and that a foreign record is answered exactly as a missing one. R27_internal_consistency.criterion: The thirty-two character lowercase hexadecimal identifier that media rows and preview tokens both carry is minted by a single helper every model calls, so the convention has one definition in source rather than a repeated literal per table.
R27_internal_consistency.evaluation_rule: The identifier is the thirty-two character lowercase hexadecimal token carried by the media row's id and by the preview token's token column. Yes if one helper mints it and both models call that helper, so the length, the case and the alphabet have one definition in source. No if each model builds its own token with its own uuid4 hex, token_hex or urandom expression, if the minting length literal appears at more than one site, or if the two tables mint by different routines.
R27_internal_consistency.rationale: The criterion explicitly rejects separate per-model `token_hex` expressions and any repeated minting-length literal. Runtime media IDs and preview tokens are minted at two distinct sites, each directly calling `secrets.token_hex(16)`, so the 32-character lowercase-hex convention does not have a single source definition.
evidence: Delivered source `app/routes.py` independently mints media IDs at line 469 with `media_id = secrets.token_hex(16)` and independently mints preview tokens at line 550 with `token = secrets.token_hex(16)`.

A source-wide grep for `secrets\.token_hex\(16\)` returned exactly those two separate minting sites in `app/routes.py`, proving that the length-setting literal `16` is repeated rather than owned by one helper.
The media value is inserted into `media.id` at lines 473–475, while the preview value is inserted into `preview_tokens.token` at lines 553–555.
`migrations/schema.sql` confirms these are the relevant columns: `media.id text PRIMARY KEY` and `preview_tokens.token text NOT NULL UNIQUE`.

A source-wide helper search found no shared helper called by both routes. `app/seed.py` has a separate deterministic `hex32(*parts)` helper used only for seeded media, while runtime media and preview creation still use their own direct `secrets.token_hex(16)` expressions.

R28_internal_consistency.criterion: Instants are held in UTC and a slug is lowercased at one boundary before it is stored or compared, and both conventions are applied identically in every model, seed routine and serialiser that touches them.
R28_internal_consistency.evaluation_rule: An instant is any stored or serialised timestamp -- created_at, published_at, expires_at -- and the boundary is the single place a slug is normalised. Yes if every timestamp is produced and stored in UTC through one convention, a slug is lowercased once at that one boundary before it is stored or compared, and every model, seed routine and serialiser applies both conventions identically. No if some modules take a naive local-time now while others take a UTC-aware one, if a slug is lowercased in a route handler in one place and in a model or the seed in another, or if any lookup compares a slug without lowercasing, so that Rives and rives could diverge.
R28_internal_consistency.rationale: The positive composite requirement is false. Although the database uses timestamptz and the explicit Python clocks are UTC-aware, timestamp values are produced by both PostgreSQL `now()` and Python `datetime.now(timezone.utc)` and serialized at separate call sites without one enforcing UTC convention. More decisively, slug lowercasing is duplicated across the write helper and several comparison/lookup sites, while seeds rely on already-lowercase literals and exact comparisons. Therefore the conventions are not applied identically through one boundary in every model/seed/serializer that touches them.
evidence: Source-wide timestamp search found all persisted timestamp columns in migrations/schema.sql as PostgreSQL timestamptz, but timestamp production is not applied through one identical convention: schema defaults and publishing use database now() (migrations/schema.sql; app/routes.py:435), while seeds produce published_at with datetime.now(timezone.utc) (app/seed.py:75, 165-211), and preview expiry is also produced in Python with datetime.now(timezone.utc) (app/routes.py:551). No connection/session

Timestamp serialisation is split across direct `.isoformat()` calls rather than a shared UTC serialiser: item_shape serialises published_at at app/routes.py:294, while preview creation serialises expires_at separately at app/routes.py:556. Thus the code does not establish one shared conversion that forces every serialised instant to UTC.

Slug handling is not a single normalization boundary. Writes call `kebab`, which strips and lowercases in app/routes.py:311-315 and is invoked independently by create (line 330), patch comparison (line 376), and slug-change (line 397). Reads then lowercase again in app/reads.py:61 and :72, and resolve_slug lowercases each lookup parameter at :108 and :114 while also applying SQL `lower(...)` to stored item and redirect slugs.

The schema only comments that the application writes lowercased slugs; it has no lowercase CHECK constraint (migrations/schema.sql items and slug_redirects definitions). Seed routines insert lowercase slug literals directly and perform exact, non-normalized slug comparisons in app/seed.py:192-194 and :213, which is a convention distinct from the route normalizer.

Runtime verification confirms mixed-case public lookups currently resolve: `/talents/RIVES` rendered Rives and `/works/THE-HALO` rendered The Halo. This demonstrates case-insensitive behavior for those paths, but source inspection shows it is achieved by repeated lookup normalization, not the required single boundary.
